title: Torfat al-Kulub and the Melody of Peace
summary: During a period of tense factional discord in the Abbasid court, two powerful factions of emirs were on the verge of armed conflict in Baghdad.
keywords: tale of the damsel torfat al-kulub
full_text:
During a period of tense factional discord in the Abbasid court, two powerful factions of emirs were on the verge of armed conflict in Baghdad.

The Caliph Harun al-Rashid hosted an imperial banquet to attempt reconciliation, but the emirs sat with cold countenances, their hands resting upon their daggers, exchanging glances of mutual hatred.

The Caliph summoned Torfat al-Kulub, a court singer of peerless musical genius, celebrated for her poetic improvisations.

Torfat al-Kulub tuned her cedarwood lute, stepped into the center of the hall, and began to sing. She did not sing of military glory or tribal triumphs; she sang an ancient, moving ballad of the Tigris river—how its waters flow from the northern snows, giving drink to the date palm and the wheat field alike, never asking whose hand planted the seed.

Her melody rose with such breathtaking tenderness, emotional purity, and soulful beauty that the stern emirs bowed their heads; tears rolled down their bearded cheeks, and their hands slipped from their daggers.

When the song concluded in reverent silence, the rival leaders stood, walked to the center of the hall, embraced as brothers, and swore an oath of eternal peace.

Harun al-Rashid rewarded the singer with three thousand dinars, declaring that her lute had accomplished what an army of fifty thousand spears could never achieve.
moral: Art and sublime poetry soften political rancor and unite divided factions in harmony.
